topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Best interests, families and IMCAs
blurb: Make best interests decisions for people with learning disabilities using the s4 checklist, involve families and carers properly, and know when an IMCA must be instructed.
question: Graham, 61, has a severe learning disability and has lived in the same care home for 30 years. He has no family or friends. He has lost weight and had two aspiration pneumonias, and the consultant proposes a gastrostomy. Graham lacks capacity to decide. What must happen?

teach.h: Deciding for someone, not about them
teach.body: When a person has been assessed as lacking capacity for a decision, anything done for them must be in their best interests (MCA s1(5)), choosing the less restrictive option where possible (s1(6)). Best interests is not what professionals think is medically best, nor what the family wants: it is what is right for this person, built from their wishes, feelings, beliefs and values. In plain English: decide as close as possible to how the person would decide.

steps.label: Valid advance decision?
steps.sub: A refusal made with capacity applies

Health and welfare LPA

teach.caption: Next of kin has no legal power to decide for an adult.

head: Section
What the decision-maker must do
rows: Not decide merely on age, appearance, condition or behaviour
Consider whether and when the person may regain capacity
Permit and encourage the person to participate
Life-sustaining treatment: not be motivated by a desire to bring about death
Consider past and present wishes (especially written ones), beliefs and values
Consult people named by the person, carers, attorneys and deputies

teach.h: Families and carers: consulted, not deciders
teach.body: Families, friends and paid carers who know the person often hold the key information: what the person enjoys, what they fear, how they have reacted before. The decision-maker must consult them where practicable (s4(7)) and weigh their views, but they do not make the decision unless they hold a health and welfare LPA or are a deputy with that authority. Where a serious disagreement cannot be resolved, mediation and then the Court of Protection are the routes.

root.label: Person lacks capacity for the decision

children.edge: Serious medical treatment (NHS) or long-term accommodation
children.label: Anyone appropriate to consult, other than paid or professional carers?
Instruct an IMCA
children.sub: Treatment may proceed first if urgent

teach.caption: MCA ss37-39. Paid support workers and professionals do not count as 'appropriate to consult' for this test.

items.label: medical treatment proposed by an NHS body (s37)
care home or local authority residential move (ss38-39)

teach.body: An independent mental capacity advocate represents the person. Their role (s36) includes supporting the person to participate as fully as possible, obtaining and evaluating information, finding out the person's likely wishes, feelings, beliefs and values, identifying alternative options, and obtaining a further medical opinion where treatment is proposed and they think one is needed. The decision-maker must take the IMCA's information into account (s37(5)). The IMCA does not make the decision.

rows.label: Clinician proposing treatment
values: Yes, if no attorney or deputy

teach.body: A gastrostomy is serious medical treatment, and Graham has no one to consult other than paid staff, so the NHS body must instruct an IMCA before it goes ahead (s37). The consultant arranges a best interests meeting. Graham is supported to take part with pictures and objects. Staff who have known him for years describe how much he loves the taste of food, and the IMCA asks for a speech and language therapy opinion on safe tastes. The decision and how his wishes were weighed are recorded.

teach.text: Two traps: paid carers ARE consulted about best interests but do NOT count as 'appropriate to consult' when deciding whether an IMCA is needed. And a learning disability is never a reason in itself to withhold treatment or make a DNACPR decision (s4(1); NHS England guidance on DNACPR and learning disability).

items: Best interests only after incapacity for that decision is shown; less restrictive option.
s4: no assumptions from condition; regain capacity?; participation; wishes, beliefs, values; consult others.
Families and carers are consulted; they decide only with an LPA or deputyship.
IMCA: serious medical treatment, hospital 28 days+, care home 8 weeks+, with nobody but paid carers to consult.
IMCA represents and can seek a further medical opinion; the decision-maker must take their information into account.

summary: You can now apply the s4 best interests checklist to people with learning disabilities, involve families, carers and attorneys in the right roles, and identify when an IMCA must be instructed and what the IMCA contributes.

A.q: An IMCA has been instructed for Sunil, 48, who has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about bowel surgery. Which of these is a function of the IMCA under MCA s36?
options: Giving consent to the surgery on Sunil's behalf
Making the final best interests decision
Obtaining a further medical opinion if needed
Acting as Sunil's deputy for his finances
A.why: s36(2)(e): an IMCA may obtain a further medical opinion where treatment is proposed and they think one should be obtained. They represent Sunil; they do not decide.

whyNot.0: An IMCA cannot consent on the person's behalf.
whyNot.1: The decision-maker makes the decision, taking the IMCA's information into account.
whyNot.3: Deputies are appointed by the Court of Protection; an IMCA is not a deputy.

A.q: A team is making a best interests decision about life-sustaining treatment for Maureen, 66, who has a learning disability and lacks capacity. Which rule from MCA s4 applies?
options: The family's view must be followed if they all agree
Treatment may be withheld if her quality of life seems poor
A court order is required before any decision is made
The decision-maker must not be motivated by a wish to bring about death
A.why: s4(5): in considering life-sustaining treatment, the decision-maker must not be motivated by a desire to bring about the person's death.

whyNot.0: Family views are weighed, but the family does not decide.
whyNot.1: Assumptions about quality of life based on her condition breach s4(1).
whyNot.2: Most best interests decisions are made without the court.

A.q: Jason, 37, has a severe learning disability, lacks capacity and has no family. He needs emergency surgery tonight for a perforated bowel. No IMCA has been instructed. What should happen?
options: Proceed in his best interests, as the treatment is urgent
Delay surgery until an IMCA has been instructed
Ask the hospital chaplain to consent on his behalf
Apply to the Court of Protection before surgery
A.why: s37(4): if treatment needs to be provided urgently, it may be provided even though an IMCA has not been instructed. It must still be in his best interests.

whyNot.1: The Act allows urgent treatment without waiting for an IMCA.
whyNot.2: Nobody can consent on behalf of an adult without legal authority.
whyNot.3: A court application is not needed for urgent treatment in his best interests.

B.q: The local authority plans to move Sandra, 58, who has a learning disability, lacks capacity and has no family, into a care home. When must an IMCA be instructed?
options: If the stay is likely to be 8 weeks or more
If the stay is likely to be 28 days or more
If the stay is likely to be 12 weeks or more
If the stay is likely to be 6 months or more
B.why: MCA s39 (and s38 for NHS-arranged care homes): an IMCA is required for a care home stay likely to be 8 weeks or more where there is nobody appropriate to consult.

whyNot.1: 28 days applies to NHS-arranged hospital stays.
whyNot.3: The threshold is 8 weeks, not 6 months.

B.q: An IMCA has been instructed for Graham, 61, who has a severe learning disability and no family. Staff at his care home have known him for 30 years. Should they also be consulted in the best interests process?
options: No, the IMCA's report replaces the views of staff
Yes, their knowledge of his wishes should be sought
No, paid carers are excluded from best interests
Yes, and they can make the decision with the IMCA
B.why: s4(7) requires consulting anyone engaged in caring for the person. Paid carers do not count as 'appropriate to consult' for the IMCA test, but their knowledge still matters.

whyNot.0: The IMCA adds to, but does not replace, other people's knowledge.
whyNot.2: Paid carers are consulted in best interests decisions.
whyNot.3: Neither staff nor the IMCA make the decision.

B.q: Rhian, 34, has a learning disability. When she had capacity she wrote in her easy read 'about me' book that she wants to stay at home if she is ill. She now lacks capacity to decide where to have treatment for an infection. How should this statement be treated?
options: Disregard it, as it is not a formal advance decision
Treat it as a legally binding refusal of hospital care
Give it particular weight as a written statement of her wishes
Follow it if her family say they agree with it
B.why: s4(6)(a): the decision-maker must consider past wishes and feelings, in particular any relevant written statement made when the person had capacity.

whyNot.0: It must be considered, even though it is not an advance decision.
whyNot.1: A statement of wishes is not a binding refusal; it is weighed in best interests.
whyNot.3: Her family's views are weighed, but they do not decide whether her wishes count.

C.q: Graham, 61, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity. He has no family or friends; care home staff have supported him for 30 years. After two aspiration pneumonias, the consultant proposes a gastrostomy. What must happen?
options: Staff who know him well decide, as they are like family
The consultant proceeds, as the gastrostomy is indicated
Instruct an IMCA and hold a best interests meeting with Graham
Apply to the Court of Protection before any further step
C.why: A gastrostomy is serious medical treatment and Graham has nobody but paid carers to consult, so an IMCA must be instructed (s37). The best interests process involves Graham (s4(4)) and those who know him.

whyNot.0: Paid staff are consulted but cannot decide, and they do not remove the IMCA duty.
whyNot.1: Clinical indication is not enough; s37 requires an IMCA and a best interests process.
whyNot.3: A court application is for unresolved disputes or specific cases, not the first step.

C.q: Phil, 55, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. A registrar suggests a DNACPR decision 'given his quality of life with a learning disability'. What should the nurse do?
options: Agree, as a severe learning disability lowers CPR success
Agree, if his sister signs the DNACPR form for him
Wait for an IMCA to decide on the DNACPR for him
Challenge it: his disability is not a reason for DNACPR
C.why: s4(1): best interests must not be decided merely on a condition. NHS England guidance states a learning disability must never be the reason for a DNACPR decision; any decision is individual and involves those who know him.

whyNot.0: A learning disability does not in itself determine CPR outcome; this is an unjustified assumption.
whyNot.1: His sister cannot consent for him, and the reasoning is still unlawful.
whyNot.2: An IMCA does not decide, and the reasoning remains the problem.

C.q: Nell, 40, has a mild learning disability. When she had capacity she made a registered health and welfare LPA appointing her brother. She now lacks capacity to decide about dental treatment under general anaesthetic. Who makes the decision?
options: The dentist, as the treating clinician
Her brother as attorney, in her best interests
An IMCA, as she now lacks capacity
Her parents, as her next of kin
C.why: A registered health and welfare attorney can make treatment decisions within the LPA's scope, acting in Nell's best interests.

whyNot.0: Where a valid attorney has authority, the attorney decides, not the clinician.
whyNot.2: An IMCA is needed where there is nobody appropriate to consult; Nell has an attorney.
whyNot.3: Next of kin has no legal power to decide for an adult.

reteach.title: Seeing the decision through their eyes
reteach.question: If Graham could step outside his disability for a moment and tell you what matters to him, what would he say? That is the question best interests tries to answer.

blocks.h: Build a picture of the person
blocks.body: Gather what Graham has said and shown in the past, what he enjoys and dislikes, his routines and values. Involve him as much as he can be involved. Ask the people who know him, paid or unpaid. If there is nobody but paid staff and the decision is serious, bring in an IMCA to stand in his corner.

blocks.text: Hospital 28 days, care home 8 weeks. The IMCA represents; the decision-maker decides.

explain.body: No assumptions from condition (s4(1)); consider regaining capacity (s4(3)); encourage participation (s4(4)); wishes, feelings, beliefs and values (s4(6)); consult others (s4(7)).

test.q: Bernard, 57, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about a hearing aid fitting. A colleague asks whether there is any point including him in the best interests meeting. What is the correct answer?
options: No, as he lacks capacity he cannot take part
Yes, he should be helped to take part as fully as he can
No, his carers can put forward his views instead
Yes, so he can sign the meeting record at the end
test.why: s4(4): the decision-maker must, so far as reasonably practicable, permit and encourage the person to participate as fully as possible.

whyNot.0: Lacking capacity for the decision does not remove the duty to involve him.
whyNot.2: Carers' views are sought too, but they do not replace his participation.
whyNot.3: Participation means real involvement in the decision, not a signature.

explain.body: Consulted where practicable (s4(7)) and their knowledge weighed. They decide only if they hold a health and welfare LPA or deputyship. Unresolved serious disputes: mediation, then the Court of Protection.

test.q: Lacey, 29, has PMLD and lacks capacity to decide about spinal surgery. Her parents, who have cared for her all her life, ask whether they will make the decision. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, parents decide for an adult child who lacks capacity
They will be consulted, but the decision-maker decides
Yes, as they are recorded as her next of kin
No, families are not involved in clinical decisions
test.why: s4(7): the decision-maker must consult those caring for Lacey and weigh their views, but parents decide only if they hold a health and welfare LPA or deputyship.

whyNot.0: Parents have no automatic legal authority over an adult.
whyNot.2: Next of kin has no legal power to decide for an adult.
whyNot.3: Families must be consulted where practicable.

explain.body: Lacks capacity AND nobody appropriate to consult other than paid or professional carers AND serious medical treatment by the NHS (s37), or an NHS-arranged hospital stay likely to last 28 days or more or care home stay of 8 weeks or more (s38), or a local authority residential move of 8 weeks or more (s39).

test.q: Pete, 52, has a learning disability, lacks capacity and has no family. The NHS arranges a hospital rehabilitation stay. When must an IMCA be instructed?
options: If the stay is likely to be 28 days or more
If the stay is likely to be 8 weeks or more
If the stay is likely to be 7 days or more
If the stay is likely to be 3 months or more
test.why: s38(3) and (9): for NHS-arranged hospital accommodation an IMCA must be instructed, where there is nobody appropriate to consult, unless the stay is likely to be less than 28 days.

whyNot.2: 7 days is not an IMCA threshold.

explain.body: Supports participation, gathers information, works out the person's likely wishes and values, identifies alternatives, and can seek a further medical opinion. The decision-maker must take their information into account.

test.q: An IMCA reports that Dilys, 63, who has a learning disability, has always refused hospital stays and that a community option exists. What must the decision-maker do with this information?
options: File it, as the IMCA's role ends with the report
Take it into account when making the decision
Follow it, as the IMCA's view is binding
Pass it to the family to make the decision
test.why: s37(5), s38(5) and s39(6): the NHS body or local authority must take into account any information given, or submissions made, by the IMCA.

whyNot.0: The information must be considered, not just filed.
whyNot.2: The IMCA's view is not binding; the decision-maker decides.
whyNot.3: The family do not decide without legal authority.
